Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory open house returns with record turnout as it navigates rocky funding future

After the event’s 2025 cancellation, scientists called it the observatory’s most important link to the public and a much-needed boost of motivation for its researchers.

By Zohar Ford / Senior Staff Photographer
Spectator spoke with several scientists at the observatory who continue to grapple with the long-term implications of drastic federal funding cuts.
By Priyanshi Poddar • October 20, 2026 at 1:24 AM

Columbia’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory held its annual open house on Saturday, opening its doors in Palisades, New York, to more than 2,500 visitors for a day of lab tours, lectures, and hands-on science exhibits amid an uncertain time for science funding.

Local families, high school students, researchers, and members of the Columbia community congregated at the observatory to engage with ongoing research projects in its largest public event of the year.

“It’s such a great event and a way to bring the community into Lamont, which I think can kind of be a little bit of a mystery or closed off from not only the Columbia community, but also the community here in the Hudson Valley,” Ian Shuman, GSAS ’26, GSAS ’29, a third-year earth and environmental sciences doctoral candidate at the observatory, told Spectator. “So I think it’s wonderful that we can welcome them back.”

The event returned after being canceled in 2025 amid financial constraints following a $400 million federal funding cut from President Donald Trump’s administration in March 2025. Steven Goldstein, CC ’76, GSAS ’81, GSAS ’86, the observatory’s interim director who made the decision to cancel last year’s event, told Spectator that at the time, “Lamont and Columbia were under the gun.”

The funding cuts triggered the cancellation of 13 grants for ongoing climate research at the observatory, according to Goldstein, and more than 70 percent of the observatory’s annual $80 million budget comes from federal research grants.

He added that because the open house “costs the equivalent of a few jobs at least,” he moved to preserve those funds for staff and research, and said that given their situation, it would be “irresponsible” to spend that money on an open house.

He said Lamont’s funding ultimately “ended up being okay” by the end of the fiscal year, and that donors “stepped up to the plate” to help cover this year’s event.

Photo by Zohar Ford / Senior Staff Photographer
Shuman quizzes visitors with a game of “Arctic Jeopardy” on how climate change is reshaping the Arctic.
Despite the event’s return, however, some researchers said funding still remains uncertain.

Kerstin Lehnert, a senior research scientist at Lamont, leads the Geoinformatics Research Group, which builds online data systems that make analyses of rocks from Earth and astromaterials available to scientists and the public. The group has operated data systems for the National Science Foundation for over 20 years, but Lehnert said it was informed that funding will end starting next year.

Through this cut, “highly valuable resources for the community, a global community actually, will go away unless we find solutions now to commercialize them,” Lehnert stressed.

“It’s dangerous for humanity to step back from fully understanding how the Earth system works,” she said, adding that she wonders about the future generations and “what their life will be if we don’t act now.”

She described the past year as “difficult, because you feel like you’re living in a bubble and science is not as appreciated as it used to be.”

Nicholas Frearson, a senior staff associate at the observatory who has worked at Lamont since 2007, works with his team to develop filtration systems that remove the microfibers and nanofibers from washing machine water, said federal funding cuts have also impacted his project.

Frearson said almost every scientist at Lamont relies on “soft money,” which comes from grants rather than guaranteed salaries, and that most of those grants come from federal agencies like the NSF and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, both of which have been hit hard by recent cuts.

Photo by Zohar Ford / Senior Staff Photographer
Frearson stands in front of the “plastic catcher” in the microplastics tent.
One NOAA-funded project Frearson works on lost about a third of its funding, he said. He and his colleagues have been able to shift their work across other projects to cover the gap, but “for some scientists, that can be pretty catastrophic”.

“Every single scientist in Lamont has been affected in some way by federal cuts recently,” he added.

Shuman said funding uncertainty has also left researchers struggling to plan their work. “There have been moments where we didn’t know if grants were going to pay out to our project,” he said, leaving them unsure whether they could cover salaries, field equipment, and logistics. This uncertainty has caused “a lot of chaos on our projects” and left researchers “not being able to plan for the future.”

Scientists described the open house as the observatory’s most important link to the public and a much-needed source of motivation for the scientists themselves.

Francesco Fiondella, GSAS ’01, Journalism ’01, director of communications and strategic content at the Climate School, who has attended the open house since 1999, said the local community “really looks forward” to the event.

He described it as an opportunity for everyone, including researchers and graduate students, to show the scientific research happening at the observatory, which he emphasized is otherwise “not a very easily accessible campus” given its 15-mile distance from Columbia’s Morningside campus.

Frearson said the event inspires both children and adults, giving visitors a look at research that has “not necessarily even gotten to the public domain yet.”

Over the course of the day, visitors interacted with research at the observatory, Terry Plank, GSAS ’93, and her development of understanding crystal clocks, a technique used by volcanologists to measure the duration that magma sits or moves underground before a volcanic eruption.

Photo by Zohar Ford / Senior Staff Photographer
Plank introduces visitors to her volcanic research outside her tent.
Plank said scientists previously believed explosive eruptions were caused by sticky magma, but her team found the key is how quickly magma rises. She told Spectator that using the clocks of crystals, her team discovered that “the most explosive eruptions are when magma rises to the surface in minutes,” which she called “the coolest thing we’ve worked on recently.”

Photo by Zohar Ford / Senior Staff Photographer
A trash can blasts into the air during a live demonstration of how volcanoes erupt.
Visitors also met Shuman, who studies how climate change affects plants and how those changes ripple out to Arctic wildlife, specifically songbirds.

He said that the Arctic is one of the ecosystems most impacted by climate change, yet it’s a “place that people in the broader community don’t think about every day.” At his booth, visitors played “Arctic Jeopardy,” and he said the best reactions came from kids “enamored by learning facts about musk ox or polar bears.”

Conversations with scientists revealed that the day mattered for them too.

Fiondella, whose wife is a researcher, said seeing everyday visitors—especially middle and high school students—amazed by their work reminds scientists why it matters and that seeing scientists from many backgrounds also helps young people picture themselves in the field.

“They come here and they say, ‘oh, this is a field that I can get into,’” Fiondella said.

Looking ahead, however, Plank said the future of the annual open house hangs in the balance because of the funding needed to host it.

Goldstein said that the event’s future depends on how science funding evolves over the next few years, which he called “a big unknown.” For now, he said Lamont has to look at it “year by year.”

For Lehnert, who has spent 30 years at Lamont, that uncertainty is hard to accept.

“Lamont is doing absolutely fundamental research for the safety, for the benefit of society,” she said. “It’s mind-boggling that we’re suddenly struggling to find the resources for that.”

Fiondella further emphasized that public outreach is crucial to Lamont as “so much of the research that we do is funded by the citizens,” stressing that the open house allows for the general public to “become educated and science-interested and science-literate.”
